title: Peter Sloterdijk
tradition: Spherology and the philosophy of anthropotechnics
keyWorks: In the World Interior of Capital (2005)
summary: Peter Sloterdijk is a German philosopher, one of the most vivid and provocative thinkers of our time. He began with a critique of modern cynicism; then, in the Spheres trilogy, he described the human being as a creature that always lives in shared "bubbles" of closeness; and in his later books, as a "practising" creature that shapes itself through repetition and training.
onEmotions: Sloterdijk sees feelings as part of the shared spaces we live in: a mood is not locked inside one person; it hangs between people, like the climate in a room. He gives great weight to "thymos" — the Greek word for pride, dignity and anger — and believes that modern culture underestimates these feelings. Sloterdijk also sees the human being as a creature of exercise: through "anthropotechnics", that is, practices of self-formation, we can change our relationship to our feelings too. For him, what matters is not suppressing emotions but learning to handle them, the way an acrobat learns to handle heights.

anxiety.text: Anxiety often feels like exposure — as if there were no walls around you. Sloterdijk offers a precise image for this feeling. In the Spheres trilogy he describes the human being as a creature that never lives simply "in the world" but always in a "sphere" — a shared space of closeness, like a bubble: family, home, language, a circle of friends. These spheres work like the soul's immune system, protecting us from the boundless outside. Modernity, according to Sloterdijk, has destroyed many of the great protective shells — for instance, the idea of a closed cosmos in which everything has its place. So anxiety is not your weakness but the understandable reaction of a creature left without its former walls. Seen this way, what helps is not a search for absolute protection but the careful building and upkeep of your own small spheres.
anxiety.practice: Draw your "bubble": who and what gives you a sense of protected space right now? Mark at least three points.

fear.text: Fear is a normal reaction to heights, the unknown, risk. In You Must Change Your Life, Sloterdijk writes a great deal about acrobats, athletes and ascetics — people who practise for years in order to do the incredible. He introduces the notion of "vertical tension": human beings always feel drawn towards something higher and harder than what they are now. The acrobat doesn't stop being afraid — she trains her relationship to fear, step by step making the impossible possible. Sloterdijk calls such practices of self-formation "anthropotechnics". Seen this way, fear is not a verdict but a sign of the height you are approaching. You don't have to defeat it in one leap: you can practise in small, manageable steps, and your body will gradually get used to it.
fear.practice: Break what you are afraid of into the smallest steps and choose the first — so small that it seems almost funny.

sadness.text: Sadness often feels as if the air around you has grown heavier. Sloterdijk would say that a mood is never locked inside one person: in Spheres he describes how people live in shared spaces where feelings are passed on and resonate, like sound in a room. He names the bond between mother and child as the first such sphere, and after it all relationships of closeness that create a shared "atmosphere". Seen this way, one could say that sadness is a change in the climate of your sphere: something in the space of closeness has shifted, grown quieter or emptier. This view lifts part of the self-blame: you haven't "broken down"; you are responding sensitively to the atmosphere. And it also points to a way: sadness is lighter when it is shared, when there is someone nearby who can hear it.
sadness.practice: Describe the "weather" in your sphere today with one image: fog, drizzle, a lull? Whom could you tell about this weather?

grief.text: Grief is one of the heaviest experiences, and it deserves gentleness. In the first volume of Spheres, titled Bubbles, Sloterdijk describes human life as fundamentally paired: from the very beginning we live not alone but in spheres created by two. When one of the two is gone, the sphere, in his image, bursts, and the one who remains finds themselves in a suddenly opened-up space. Seen this way, grief is not only sorrow but the loss of the very form in which you lived. That is why it is so hard to breathe and so unclear where "inside" is now. This view helps you understand that the slowness of grief is natural: a new sphere can't be built quickly. It comes together gradually — from memory, from people nearby, from habits that begin to warm you again.
grief.practice: Name one small thing — a place, a ritual, a voice — near which you feel at least a little warmer right now. Stay with it for a few minutes.

loneliness.text: Loneliness in the modern world is not only a personal story. In the third volume of Spheres, titled Foams, Sloterdijk describes modern society as a foam: a multitude of separate bubbles that touch at their walls but rarely merge. He speaks of "co-isolation" — being isolated together: we live side by side, behind the thin walls of apartments, and yet each in our own bubble. The one-person apartment, for Sloterdijk, is one of the characteristic forms of our era. Seen this way, your loneliness is partly caused by the very architecture of modern life, not by your "inability". But foam has a good side too: the bubbles touch. You can notice these touches — a neighbour, a voice on the phone, a shared window onto the courtyard — and little by little make the walls thinner.
loneliness.practice: Recall all the brief "touches" with other people today — even a nod or a message. Choose one that could be extended a little.

anger.text: People are often ashamed of anger, but Sloterdijk suggests taking it more seriously. His book Rage and Time opens with a reminder: the first word of European literature is "wrath" — it is the word that opens Homer's Iliad. Sloterdijk believes that modern culture, absorbed in the psychology of desire, has underestimated "thymos" — the Greek word for pride, self-respect and righteous anger. Seen this way, anger often says: "I have not been treated as I deserve." It is a legitimate energy. At the same time, Sloterdijk shows how dangerous it is to store anger in "rage banks" — to save it up for future retribution. You can respect your anger as the voice of dignity and at the same time not keep it for years, but look for somewhere to invest its force.
anger.practice: Complete the sentence: "My anger is protecting my right to…" What one small action could support this right?

quote.text: Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus…
quote.author: Homer
quote.source: The Iliad, Book I (trans. Samuel Butler)

shame.text: Shame makes you shrink and hide. In Critique of Cynical Reason, Sloterdijk offers an unexpected ally — the ancient philosopher Diogenes, who lived in a barrel and openly mocked the proprieties of Athens. Sloterdijk calls his stance "kynicism", as opposed to modern "cynicism": a bodily, cheerful impudence with which the little person answers the puffed-up seriousness of power and convention. From Sloterdijk's point of view, much of what we are taught to be ashamed of is social masks, not the truth about a person. This doesn't mean shame is always false. But it can be checked: whose gaze on me is this? Sometimes a drop of Diogenes' impudence is a useful answer to shame — a smile that reminds you that you have the right to be a living human being, not a flawless statue.
shame.practice: Ask yourself: whose eyes am I looking at myself through right now? Write down a name or a role — and notice that this is not the only possible gaze.

guilt.text: Guilt shows that you measure yourself against something important — people, rules, your own expectations. In You Must Change Your Life, Sloterdijk describes the human being as a "practising creature": we shape ourselves through repetition, and every action is also an exercise that strengthens or weakens a particular skill. Seen this way, one could say that a mistake is not a final verdict but an unsuccessful attempt, after which another is possible. Sloterdijk is less interested in condemnation than in how people actually change and become better in practice. In this light, guilt can become not endless self-punishment but a starting point for a new exercise: what can I do differently tomorrow — in something small and concrete?
guilt.practice: Put into words one small "exercise" for tomorrow that answers this guilt with action rather than self-criticism.

envy.text: Envy is a painful feeling in which desire and wounded pride are mixed. In You Must Change Your Life, Sloterdijk speaks of "vertical tension": people always see someone "above" them — a master, a champion, someone who can do more. This tension, for Sloterdijk, is the engine of human self-improvement, the source of all training and learning. Seen this way, one could say that envy is a clumsy, painful form of the same vertical pull: you see the height and feel the distance to it sharply. In Rage and Time he shows how such a feeling can sour into ressentiment — a hidden grudge. But it can also become training. The point is not to stop noticing someone else's height, but to turn it from a reproach into a landmark.
envy.practice: Name the skill or quality you see in the person you envy. What would be the very first exercise in that direction?

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy can resemble a weary "so what". In Critique of Cynical Reason, Sloterdijk described this state as a mass phenomenon: the modern person understands everything, sees the falseness, knows that much is meaningless — and still goes on doing what they were doing. This isn't stupidity or laziness, but a particular tiredness of those who know and can't see how to live otherwise. Seen this way, your emptiness may be not a personal defect but a reflection of the general climate of the era. Sloterdijk set against this "kynicism" — a lively, bodily, laughing response to the world. For him, the way out of emptiness lies not in a new grand ideology but in feeling the body again, a joke, the simple audacity of living.
emptiness.practice: Do one simple bodily action — stretch, step outside, splash your face with cold water — and notice what has changed, even by one percent.

confusion.text: Confusion is a natural state when there is no shared picture of the world. Sloterdijk explains why this is so in our era. In the second volume of Spheres, Globes, he describes how for centuries people lived inside great, all-uniting images — a single cosmos, a single faith, a single empire, where everything had its place. Modernity destroyed this great sphere. In the third volume, Foams, the world appears as a multitude of small bubbles with no single centre. Seen this way, confusion is not your inability to figure things out but an accurate perception of a world that has no one middle. This can even be freeing: you don't need to look for the one true picture. It's enough to understand which of your spheres you are standing in right now, and take a step from inside it.
confusion.practice: Choose one of your "spheres" — work, family, friendship — and ask: what is clear to me here right now? Write down one clear thing.

fatigue.text: Tiredness and burnout are not weakness but a signal of overload. In his essay Stress and Freedom, Sloterdijk describes modern societies as communities held together by shared tension: news, worries and urgencies are passed continuously from person to person, creating a collective agitation. Seen this way, part of your tiredness is not only personal: you live inside a large nervous system that almost never rests. At the same time, Sloterdijk thinks of the human being as a "practising creature", and any coach knows that training without recovery is destructive. One could say that anthropotechnics — the art of self-formation — includes pausing and dropping what is unnecessary. Rest, then, is not quitting the race but part of the very practice that makes you yourself.
fatigue.practice: Disconnect for ten minutes from all news and work streams and simply notice how your breathing gradually changes.

boredom.text: Boredom seems a trifle, but Sloterdijk saw such states as a feature of the era. In In the World Interior of Capital he describes the modern affluent world as a vast greenhouse — a "crystal palace" of comfort where life is made as easy as possible. Such relief is a great achievement, but it has a flip side: when almost nothing resists, the feeling that anything matters disappears. From Sloterdijk's point of view, one could say that boredom is a lack of "vertical tension" — the pull towards the difficult and the high that makes life tense in a good sense. Boredom, then, is not empty time but a hint: you may be missing a challenge within your reach. It can be a very small exercise that you choose yourself.
boredom.practice: Set yourself a small challenge for the next fifteen minutes — a little harder than usual, but doable. Give it a try.

joy.text: For Sloterdijk, joy is not frivolity but an important force. In Critique of Cynical Reason he sets against the gloomy, all-knowing cynicism the ancient "kynicism" of Diogenes — a philosophy that laughs, talks back, delights in the body and the sun. There is a famous story of how Diogenes asked Alexander the Great to step aside because he was blocking his sun. For Sloterdijk, this gesture contains a whole philosophy: the joy of simple existence is stronger than any greatness. Seen this way, joy doesn't need to be earned or justified. It can be a form of resistance to gloom, a quiet "yes" to life amid its difficulties. You can let yourself rejoice simply and bodily — in the sun, food, movement — and not apologise for it.
joy.practice: Find a minute of "Diogenes' sun" today: a simple bodily pleasure that you enjoy without trying to achieve anything.

quote.author: Diogenes of Sinope (as tradition has it)
quote.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI

love.text: For Sloterdijk, love and tenderness are the foundation of human existence. The first volume of Spheres is built on the idea that a human being is never originally alone: we come into the world already inside relationships, in a "bubble" of closeness with another. These are the spaces Sloterdijk calls "spheres" — not places on a map but a shared air that two people create by resonating with each other. Seen this way, love is not just a feeling inside you but a joint construction: together you create an atmosphere in which both of you can breathe. This helps you see tenderness not as weakness but as the work of sustaining a shared world. And it also explains why love needs small things so much — gestures, a voice, attention: these are what the walls of the sphere are made of.
love.practice: Recall one small thing that makes the "air" you share with someone close warmer. Do it today.

gratitude.text: Gratitude is the recognition that someone has supported you. Sloterdijk reminds us how deeply true this is. In You Must Change Your Life he shows that everything we can do has been handed down to us through long chains of teachers, coaches and mentors — through traditions of practice stretching back thousands of years. You are the heir of many people who once learned and taught. In addition, in The Taking Hand and the Giving Side, Sloterdijk reflected on generosity as a feeling connected with pride and dignity rather than with loss. Seen this way, gratitude and generosity are two sides of one movement: what you have received, you want to pass on. You can give thanks not only with words but also by one day becoming someone's teacher.
gratitude.practice: Name one person who once taught you something important. What part of it could you teach someone else?

hope.text: For Sloterdijk, hope is bound up with practice. The title of his book You Must Change Your Life is a line from a poem by Rilke: the poet looks at an ancient torso of Apollo and suddenly feels a demand addressed to himself. Sloterdijk sees in this call the central signal of human life: we are able to change — through exercises, repetitions, small daily efforts. Seen this way, hope is not passive waiting for everything to sort itself out but the knowledge that you are a creature that can practise. Change doesn't require a heroic leap; it is built from what you do again and again. To hope is to trust the power of small repetitions.
hope.practice: Choose one tiny action that you are ready to repeat every day for the whole of next week. Write it down.

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a longing for what was home. Sloterdijk gives this feeling an almost cosmic scale. In Spheres he describes how human beings lose their protective shells again and again: each of us leaves the first, closest space — the maternal one — and civilisation as a whole has lost the picture of a closed, cosy cosmos in which everyone had their place. Seen this way, nostalgia is the memory of a sphere in which it was warm and understandable. This feeling is not naive: it points to a genuine human need to be "inside". Sloterdijk doesn't propose returning to the past — that is impossible. But nostalgia can suggest which qualities of the lost sphere you want to recreate now: warmth, rhythm, voices, smells.
nostalgia.practice: Name three qualities of the place or time you miss. Which of them could you recreate, even a little, today?

craving.text: A craving is a sharp "I want it right now", and it can be very strong; there is nothing shameful in it. Sloterdijk helps us see it more broadly. In In the World Interior of Capital he describes the modern world as a "crystal palace" — a vast greenhouse of comfort where almost everything is available at once and almost without effort. Such a world trains us to expect desires to be fulfilled instantly, and a craving partly arises from this very atmosphere, not only from you. And in You Must Change Your Life he describes the human being as a creature of exercise: we become what we repeat. Seen this way, every time you notice a wave of craving and let it rise and ebb away without following it right away, that is a small exercise, like an acrobat's step on the tightrope. Not a heroic feat, but training in which every repetition counts.
craving.practice: When a wave of craving comes, watch it the way an acrobat watches the wind: where it is in your body, whether it is growing, whether it is starting to subside.

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure but a loop that life has gradually been built into, and it is hard to get out of. Sloterdijk offers an unfamiliar but liberating view of it. In You Must Change Your Life he argues that the human being is a creature that is always practising: habits, rituals and repetitions shape us, even when we don't notice. Seen this way, addiction can be understood as an exercise nobody consciously chose: a repetition that has long trained the body and the days around a single point. This matters: what took shape through repetition can also be reshaped through repetition — slowly, through other exercises. Sloterdijk stresses that no one practises alone: every practice has teachers, companions, communities. So getting out of the loop is not a leap of will but the gradual building of a new "sphere" around yourself.
addiction.practice: Write down one small habit you could repeat every day alongside this loop — a walk, a phone call, a cup of tea. If you like, think about whom you could talk to about it: someone close to you, or a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: A hangover can be twofold: the body aches, and inside there is anxiety, shame, fragments of memory. It's a hard morning, and it deserves gentleness, not new reproaches. Sloterdijk describes the human being as a creature living in "spheres" — shared bubbles of mood. An evening gathering creates such a bubble: shared noise, warmth, a feeling that anything goes. In the morning the bubble bursts, and you are left alone with its fragments. Part of the morning anxiety is the shock of a sudden change of climate. Sloterdijk also writes a great deal about "thymos" — the Greek word for pride and self-respect. A moral hangover strikes precisely at it. From Sloterdijk's point of view, dignity doesn't need to be finished off with self-punishment: it can be calmly restored — through small deeds that give you back your self-respect.
hangover.practice: Do one simple act of self-care — a glass of water, a shower, an open window — and mark it as the first step of recovery, not as a punishment.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is a vivid feeling: the world suddenly opens up, and everything seems possible. There's no need to hurry to spoil it. Sloterdijk has the notion of "vertical tension": people, in his view, always reach upwards — towards something higher and more incredible than their ordinary life. Euphoria is the moment when this vertical is felt in the body: as if you had been lifted to a height from which you can see far. Sloterdijk loves images of performers and acrobats: whoever works at height delights in it, but knows that height is a place, not a permanent address. Seen this way, you can live euphoria fully and at the same time remember what exactly opened up to you from above. Then its trace will stay with you even after the descent.
euphoria.practice: Write down one sentence right now: what did you see "from the height" — what possibility, desire or thought do you want to keep?

crash.text: After a high, a celebration or a success, a sharp drop sometimes follows — a "comedown". It can feel almost like a betrayal by your own mood, and that is very understandable. Sloterdijk describes the human being through "vertical tension": we reach upwards, towards the incredible, towards moments when life rises above the ordinary. But every vertical also means a descent. Drawing on his book You Must Change Your Life, one could say that any serious practice — from sport to monastic life — rests not on peaks but on the everyday: on regular training. Seen this way, the drop is not proof that the high was a deception, nor is it a verdict. It is the return to the ground after a height, and on the ground you can find your footing again: rhythm, simple tasks, people nearby.
crash.practice: Choose one small everyday task — make the bed, go for a walk, cook a meal — and do it slowly, as a return to solid ground.

panic.text: A panic attack is truly frightening: your heart pounds, you seem not to be getting enough air, it feels as though something irreparable is about to happen. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes, but from the inside that is hard to believe. Sloterdijk has the notion of "explication" — bringing into the light what usually remains an unnoticed background. In Spheres he shows that air, breathing and the atmosphere around us usually just are there, and we don't notice them — until something is disrupted. Panic is exactly such a moment: the background of life suddenly becomes explicit and frightening. Seen this way, you can try to give your breathing back its role as an unnoticed support — not fighting it, but gently lengthening the out-breath and letting the background become background again.
panic.practice: Put both feet on the floor, feel its firmness, and take a few breaths with the out-breath longer than the in-breath. Name aloud three objects you can see around you.

dread.text: Existential dread — "what's the point of it all", the thought of finitude, the sense of an abyss beneath your feet — is one of the heaviest experiences, and the fact that you have it speaks of depth, not of something broken. In the Spheres trilogy, Sloterdijk explains where this dread comes from in our era. For a long time people lived inside an imagined closed cosmos — a vast "sphere" in which everything had its place. The modern age shattered this shell, and human beings found themselves facing an infinite space without walls. Pascal already expressed this chill in his famous line about infinite spaces. But Sloterdijk takes an important step: since the great dome no longer holds us, people build small spheres again and again — friendship, love, shared work, homes. Meaning doesn't fall from the sky; it is created together, inside warm bubbles of closeness.
dread.practice: Name one "small sphere" that is holding you, even a little, right now — a person, a place, a task. Stay with this thought for a minute.

quote.text: The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me.
quote.author: Blaise Pascal

fomo.text: The fear of missing out — the feeling that real life is happening somewhere else and you are not there — is a very familiar feeling of our time. Sloterdijk describes modern society as a "foam": a huge multitude of separate bubble-worlds that touch at their walls. An important feature of foam is that it has no centre. The old world had a capital, a palace, a main square — a place where "everything happens". In foam there are no such places: each bubble is its own small centre of the world. Screens let us peer through the walls into thousands of other bubbles, and from inside they seem brighter, because we see their lit-up shop windows, not their ordinary days. Seen this way, the "right place" simply doesn't exist. There is your bubble — and you can make yourself at home in it.
fomo.practice: Describe in three sentences what is happening in your "bubble" right now: sounds, light, people or things nearby.

sleepless.text: Insomnia and 3 a.m. thoughts are exhausting: the world is asleep, and your head is working at full power. In Stress and Freedom, Sloterdijk observes that large societies are held together largely by shared worries: news, problems and concerns constantly circulate and keep everyone on edge. At night this shared stream doesn't switch off — it goes on humming inside you. So the nightly carousel of thoughts is partly not your personal inability to "switch off" but an echo of the anxious climate of the era. And in the first volume of Spheres, Sloterdijk describes a person's earliest, most intimate spaces — those in which we were sheltered and bound to another. Seen this way, what may help at night is not a fight for sleep but a small return to such a shelter: warmth, darkness, the feeling of a safe cocoon.
sleepless.practice: If you can't sleep, wrap yourself up more snugly and tell yourself: "Now is not the time for deciding; now is the time for shelter." Write the worrying thought down in one line and leave it until morning.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds especially deeply because it comes from where you felt safe. Sloterdijk helps us understand why it hurts so much. In the first volume of Spheres he writes that close relationships create a shared inner space — a bubble for two or for several, where people breathe the same air of trust. We build ourselves inside such bubbles. Betrayal is a puncture from within: what collapses is not only your relationship to the person but also part of your inner world, which was shared. Hence the feeling that the ground has gone from under your feet. Sloterdijk also values "thymos" — self-respect and righteous anger. Seen this way, your pain and indignation are legitimate: this is how dignity declares that it has been wronged. In time you can build new spheres — with experience now, but without giving up on closeness.
betrayal.practice: Write one sentence about what was valuable to you in this shared space. It is yours, and it can't be taken away along with the relationship.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is agonising: fear of loss, pain and anger are mixed in it. Sloterdijk describes closeness as a "sphere" — a shared space for two that works like an immune system: it protects from the cold and indifference of the outside world. Seen this way, one could say that jealousy is this immune system's alarm signal: it seems a breach has appeared in the wall of your shared bubble. The reaction is understandable — you are protecting something vital to you. But Sloterdijk also shows something else: spheres live not by being airtight but by constant shared "breathing" — attention, conversations, shared rituals. The wall of the bubble can't be held by control; two people hold it together. So you can hear jealousy as a pointer to what matters to you, and as an occasion to talk about the bond itself.
jealousy.practice: Ask yourself: what exactly am I afraid of losing in our shared space? Write it down in a word or two.

resentment.text: An old grievance is a pain you carry with you, sometimes for years. Sloterdijk has a book in which this theme is central — Rage and Time. He shows that resentment and anger are tied to "thymos" — self-respect: it hurts us when we are treated unfairly, and that is natural. But Sloterdijk also notes a danger: anger can be accumulated like money, saved up for the future — he even speaks of "rage banks". Accumulated resentment becomes capital that lies like a heavy weight and demands ever new investments. Seen this way, resentment is nothing to be ashamed of, nor does it need to be forcibly "forgiven". You can acknowledge that your dignity is in the right — and at the same time gradually stop giving the grievance all your time, bringing your energy back into the present.
resentment.practice: Write: "I was treated unfairly when…" — and finish it. Then a second line: "Today I want to invest my time in…"

heartbreak.text: A breakup can feel as though you have been cut in half. Sloterdijk explains why this is no exaggeration. In the first volume of Spheres he argues that the human being originally exists not alone but "in twos": even before birth we live in a shared space with another, and all our lives we look for such closeness again. A person close to you becomes your "complement" — part of the sphere inside which you feel like yourself at all. When the relationship ends, the bubble bursts, and you are left under the open sky. So the pain of a broken heart is not weakness but the honest reaction of a creature made for closeness. Seen this way, healing lies not in becoming a self-sufficient loner but in gradually, unhurriedly building spaces of warmth again — with friends, loved ones, with yourself.
heartbreak.practice: Note one place or one person today near whom you feel a little warmer — and stay there, or with them, a little longer than usual.

impostor.text: Impostor syndrome is the fear that you are about to be exposed: others think you know what you're doing, but you know you're just holding on. Sloterdijk suggests looking at this differently. In You Must Change Your Life he describes the human being as a "practising" creature: all our skills — from speech to a profession — are not given by nature but trained through repetition. Every master was once an apprentice and in many ways remains one. The "vertical tension" Sloterdijk writes about means that we always reach for a level a little above where we are. Seen this way, the feeling "I'm not good enough" is not proof of fraud but the natural feeling of someone walking a tightrope and still training. The impostor pretends; the practitioner learns. And the fact that you notice your gaps so honestly points rather to the second.
impostor.practice: Write down three skills you once didn't have and have since trained. This is your personal history of practice.

self_hatred.text: Self-hatred and an inner critic that never falls silent are among the most exhausting states. It's important to say right away: the critic's voice is not the truth about you. In You Must Change Your Life, Sloterdijk observes that everyone who practises is, as it were, split in two: one part trains, the other is trained. This is the normal make-up of a human being. But trainers vary. A good coach demands, but also takes care of the person they work with: without that, no athlete could endure. The inner critic is a coach who only shouts and humiliates, and under such a coach nobody gets better. Sloterdijk also insists on the value of "thymos" — the healthy dignity every person needs. Seen this way, you can refuse to accept the critic's verdict and try changing the tone of your inner voice: not "you're worthless", but "let's try again, I'm here with you".
self_hatred.practice: Write down one sentence your inner critic is saying right now, and next to it — how a kind but demanding coach would say the same thing.

helplessness.text: Helplessness is a heavy feeling, when it seems that nothing depends on you. Sloterdijk knows this trap well. In Critique of Cynical Reason he describes modern cynicism as "enlightened false consciousness": we understand everything about the world's injustice, yet feel that nothing can be changed, and wearily go on living as before. This is not your personal weakness — it is the mood of a whole era. Against it Sloterdijk sets the ancient "kynicism" of Diogenes: the philosopher who lived in a barrel had neither power nor money, yet kept his dignity and freedom of gesture even before Alexander the Great. Seen this way, even when the big things are beyond your power, the small ones remain: your tone, your step, your space nearby. Helplessness before the world doesn't cancel strength within your own sphere.
helplessness.practice: Divide a sheet of paper into two parts: "not in my power" and "in my power today". In the second column write down at least one very small thing.

procrastination.text: Procrastination is when a task hangs over you and you can't get started, and shame quickly piles on. Sloterdijk named his book after a line from Rilke's poem "Archaic Torso of Apollo": "You must change your life." The poet stands before an ancient statue, and the perfection of the stone addresses him as a demand. Sloterdijk sees in this "vertical tension" — the call of something higher. But the call has a flip side: when a task seems like a summit, it's frightening to approach. The book's main lesson is that every summit is reached through practice, that is, through repeating small steps. No one starts with a record: an athlete starts with a warm-up. Seen this way, "I can't get started" often means "the goal is too high for a first step". What helps is not pressuring yourself but shrinking the step to the size of a warm-up.
procrastination.practice: Choose the tiniest "warm-up" step towards the task — open the file, write one line — and do only that, demanding nothing more of yourself.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home — emigration, a move, the ground slipping from under your feet — is a deep upheaval, and it's natural to grieve it. Sloterdijk believes that a human being never lives simply "somewhere on the map": we live in a "sphere" — a space of language, smells, familiar faces, shared jokes. A move destroys not only an address but this whole invisible bubble, which is why it feels like losing your footing. And yet for Sloterdijk what matters most in a sphere is not the land but the closeness that people create with one another. It's no accident that Heidegger, with whom Sloterdijk argued a great deal, called language, not a place, our home. Seen this way, one could say that a sphere can partly be carried with you — in your native tongue, recipes, rituals — and slowly rebuilt where you are now.
uprooted.practice: Recall one small thing from your "old sphere" — a word, a dish, a song — and find a way to let it into your new space today.

quote.text: Language is the house of Being. In its home man dwells.
quote.author: Martin Heidegger

overload.text: Information overload, an endless feed in which everything is important and nothing ever ends, is an exhausting state, and it says nothing about your weakness. Sloterdijk describes spheres as immune systems: every living space — from a cell to a home — exists thanks to a membrane that lets some things in and keeps others out. Without a membrane there is no life, only a flood. In Stress and Freedom he shows how shared news and worries circulate continuously and keep whole societies on edge. The endless feed is a world in which the walls of your bubble have become almost transparent. Seen this way, tiredness from the stream is a healthy signal: your immune system is asking you to restore the membrane. A filter is not an escape from the world but a condition for living in it.
overload.practice: Choose one "membrane" for today: an hour without the feed, notifications off in one app, or one closed tab — and notice how the feeling changes.

unreality.text: The feeling that everything around you, or you yourself, is somehow not real is a strange and unsettling experience that is hard to talk about. Sloterdijk takes it seriously. In his book Weltfremdheit ("Strangeness to the World") he reflects that the world has never been entirely self-evident for human beings: people have always lived on the border between immersion in the world and looking at it as if from outside. And in Spheres he shows that our sense of reality rests on shared spaces — on people, voices, the familiar climate around us. Seen this way, one could say that when these supports weaken, the world may start to seem like a stage set. The feeling of unreality, then, is not a breakdown but a sign that the "bubble" has grown thin. The way back runs through simple things: touch, the sound of another person's voice, warmth.
unreality.practice: Touch three objects with different textures — something cold, something soft, something rough — and name aloud what you feel.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful — mountains, the night sky, music, a cathedral — is one of the strongest human experiences. Sloterdijk would call it an encounter with "vertical tension": the moment when you suddenly sense that there is something higher, greater and more incredible than the ordinary course of days. The Rilke poem that gave his book You Must Change Your Life its title describes exactly this kind of awe: a person stands before an ancient statue and feels that it is looking at him. In the second volume of Spheres, Globes, Sloterdijk shows how for centuries people built domes and images of the heavens in order to live beneath the immense without getting lost in it. Seen this way, awe is a rare moment when your small sphere touches the great one. You can simply savour it.
awe.practice: Stay for a minute with whatever filled you with awe, without photographing or explaining anything. Then write down one word that remains.

relief.text: Relief is when a load you have been carrying is suddenly lifted, and your body breathes out on its own. For Sloterdijk, "relief" is almost a philosophical term. Following the philosophical anthropologist Arnold Gehlen, he speaks of "unburdening": the human being is a creature that constantly invents ways of taking some of life's weight off itself — tools, houses, customs, technology. In In the World Interior of Capital, Sloterdijk describes all of modernity as a vast project of relief. He sees dangers in it too, but the striving for relief itself is, for him, deeply human. Seen this way, your relief is not a trifle, nor a reason to go looking for the next worry right away. It is a moment when life has become a little lighter, and it is worth living fully, with your body: your shoulders, your breathing, your gait.
relief.practice: Notice where in your body the relief is felt most strongly, and take one slow breath out, letting that place relax a little more.

calm.text: Calm is a rare and precious state: nothing is urgent, it's quiet inside. Sloterdijk often speaks of spheres as climates: every space we live in has its own atmosphere, its own air, its own temperature of mood. People, in his view, have always been masters of "air-conditioning" — creating spaces around themselves where one can breathe calmly: a hearth, a home, a circle of loved ones. Calm, from this point of view, is the moment when the climate of your sphere has become even and mild. It isn't emptiness or laziness but an achievement — yours, and that of the people, things and places that create a good atmosphere around you. You can treasure it without analysing too much, simply noticing: right here, right now, I can breathe easily.
calm.practice: Look around and name three things that are creating this calm — light, a sound, an object. Silently thank them.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is the moment when thoughts and images seem to arrive by themselves and you want to make things. In the first volume of Spheres, Sloterdijk reminds us that the ancients understood this differently from us: for the Romans, each person had their own "genius" — a companion spirit that accompanies and whispers. For Sloterdijk, these images are not mere superstition but an accurate feeling: even in the loneliest creative moment a person is not quite alone; they live paired with something — a voice, a tradition, a beloved book, a conversation partner. Inspiration, seen this way, is not the achievement of a solitary "I" but an encounter within your sphere. And You Must Change Your Life adds: inspiration becomes work when practice takes it up. You can rejoice in the flash — and give it a footing in a small regular action.
inspiration.practice: Write down where you think this inspiration came from — a person, a book, a place. Silently thank this "companion" and take one small step towards what you have in mind.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is awkward to admit, but almost everyone knows it: someone stumbled, and for a moment you felt lighter inside. In You Must Change Your Life, Sloterdijk describes "vertical tension": people constantly feel that someone stands higher — more successful, more talented, happier. This tension is tiring. From Sloterdijk's point of view, one could say that schadenfreude is an instant discharge of this tension: someone else's fall shortens the distance for a second, and you don't have to reach upwards. In Rage and Time he shows how a wounded "thymos" — self-respect — seeks relief. There's nothing monstrous in this. But schadenfreude gives only brief relief, and the height that troubles you remains. It's more honest to ask what vertical is pressing on you so hard.
schadenfreude.practice: Complete the sentence: "I felt lighter because next to them I feel lower when it comes to…"

contempt.text: Contempt gives a sense of height and safety: I'm above this. It's an understandable defence. Sloterdijk devoted an essay to this theme, The Contempt of the Masses: he reflects on how, in a society of universal equality, the desire to be different, to be "above" others, doesn't disappear, and how it seeks an outlet in hidden disdain. For Sloterdijk, the need for distinction is connected with "thymos" — the striving for dignity and recognition. Seen this way, one could say that contempt is thymos protecting its dignity by belittling someone else. Sloterdijk doesn't propose giving up the vertical altogether: striving for the best in yourself is natural. But the vertical, in his view, is fruitful when it pulls you yourself upwards, not when it pushes someone else down.
contempt.practice: Ask yourself: what dignity of mine is this contempt protecting? Write down the answer in one sentence.

disgust.text: Disgust is a strong bodily reaction: to pull away, to close up, to keep something out. It can arise towards people, situations and yourself, and nobody chooses it. In Spheres, Sloterdijk describes every living space as an immune system: a bubble of closeness, a home, a community hold together thanks to a membrane that decides what to let in and what to leave outside. From Sloterdijk's point of view, one could say that disgust is one of the most ancient immune responses, a guard at the border of your sphere. It protects, and that makes sense. But an immune system can also be mistaken, reacting to something safe as if it were a threat. When disgust is directed at yourself, it resembles a defence turning against its own. There's no need to be ashamed of such a reaction — it's worth taking a closer look at it.
disgust.practice: Ask yourself: what is this disgust protecting me from? Write down the answer, and next to it — whether there is really any danger there.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge usually grows from a real hurt, and it has a right to be heard. In Rage and Time, Sloterdijk describes how anger need not be spent at once but can be accumulated — he calls this "rage banks". Revenge is one such banking operation: the hurt is set aside for the future, and it "accrues interest", demanding compensation year after year. Sloterdijk sees a danger in this: the depositor gradually becomes bound to the deposit and lives for the payback. Seen this way, one could say that the wish for revenge speaks of a wounded "thymos" — your dignity, which has not received recognition. This dignity is real and important. But it can be restored without handing your life over for safekeeping in the bank of grievance.
revenge.practice: Write down what exactly in your dignity was wounded. Think about what could restore it without involving the person who hurt you.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those close to you, which you are later ashamed of, is a very human experience. In the first volume of Spheres, Sloterdijk describes closeness as a shared "bubble": a space in which two or more people live, breathe the same air and feel each other's moods. In such a bubble there is no distance to soften collisions: every irritation immediately becomes the climate of the whole room. From Sloterdijk's point of view, one could say that anger at loved ones is not proof of a lack of love but a sign of how closely your spheres are intertwined. Anger gives no right to wound, but it doesn't make you bad either. Sloterdijk sees the human being as a creature of exercise: coming back to someone close after an outburst is an exercise too, and each time it gets a little easier.
anger_at_loved.practice: After an outburst, air the room or step outside for a minute. Then say one sentence about what you were really feeling.

ambivalence.text: Loving someone close and at the same time being unable to stand them is hard, but it doesn't mean something is wrong with you. Sloterdijk describes two needs that live in everyone. In the first volume of Spheres he shows that the human being originally exists "in twos" and seeks closeness all their life. And in the third volume, Foams, he describes the modern person, who also needs a separate cell of their own, their own corner, their own space. From Sloterdijk's point of view, one could say that mixed feelings towards someone close are a clash of these two needs: you are drawn into the shared bubble and at the same time want a membrane of your own. Both feelings are legitimate. The question is not which of them is "real" but how to arrange a space with room for both closeness and separateness.
ambivalence.practice: Write down what you are missing more right now with this person — closeness or space of your own.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, or after a seriously ill loved one has died, is often accompanied by shame. But relief and love can exist together. Sloterdijk describes close relationships as a shared sphere — a space in which people hold each other. When one person is seriously ill, or a relationship has long been strained, this sphere becomes a place of constant care, worry, vigilance. For years you kept it up with your own strength. From Sloterdijk's point of view, one could say that relief is the natural reaction of a creature that has long held up a heavy structure and can finally lower its arms. It doesn't cancel the fact that you loved. Relief is a sign of how much you carried, not of how little you loved.
guilty_relief.practice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up, and tell yourself: "I held on for a long time. Now I can breathe out."

indifference.text: Sometimes something "should" move you, but inside it's empty, and that feels awkward. In Critique of Cynical Reason, Sloterdijk describes a particular state of the modern person: we know far more about the world's troubles than ever before, but this knowledge often doesn't turn into feeling. He calls cynicism "enlightened false consciousness" and explains that it is partly a defence: it is impossible to respond to everything. And in Stress and Freedom he shows that people live in a constant stream of alarm signals. From Sloterdijk's point of view, one could say that indifference is not always coldness but often a tired membrane that has stopped letting things through. It doesn't need to be broken by force. Sometimes, when the load eases, sensitivity comes back by itself.
indifference.practice: Ask yourself: how much that is heavy have I let into myself over the last few days? Give yourself a little quiet today.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything and run away — from work, a city, a role — is understandable when life has turned into constant pressure. In Stress and Freedom, Sloterdijk recalls an episode from Rousseau's life: the philosopher lies in a boat on a lake, surrendering to the rocking of the waves, and feels completely free, released from all obligations. For Sloterdijk, this is an image of a particular kind of freedom — the capacity to step back for a while from the "stress community" we are all built into. Seen this way, one could say that the dream of escape is a longing for such stepping back. It is legitimate. Sloterdijk doesn't say whether you should leave; he shows that even this inner retreat is already a form of freedom, one you can practise little by little.
escape.practice: Find ten minutes when you owe nobody anything. Spend them like Rousseau in the boat: just observe.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone unavailable or "the wrong one" can be unsettling: as if something were pulling you against your will. In the first volume of Spheres, Sloterdijk explores the history of how people have explained the mysterious pull between them: from ancient ideas of fascination to Mesmer's "animal magnetism" in the 18th century. For him, these are different attempts to describe the same thing — that human beings are originally open to the influence of others, able to resonate with them, almost like one sound with another. Seen this way, one could say that attraction is not a decision or an action but a resonance: something in the other has echoed in you. On its own it demands nothing. You can look with interest at what in you is resonating with this person.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down which part of you comes alive near this person. Where else in your life could this note sound?

social_anxiety.text: The fear of people and their judgement can turn even a brief meeting into an ordeal. It is a very common feeling. In Foams, Sloterdijk describes modern people as inhabitants of separate little bubbles: each lives in their own cell, behind a thin wall, and going out into shared space means passing through a membrane, with all its changes of pressure. Seen this way, one could say that nervousness when meeting people is a natural reaction to a change of atmosphere, not a sign that you are somehow lacking. Sloterdijk sees the human being as a creature of exercise: all skills, including social ones, are formed through repetition rather than born ready-made. Anxiety doesn't need to be defeated in one leap. You can train in small steps, as in any art.
social_anxiety.practice: Choose one small "exercise" for today — for example, asking a shop assistant something. Note that you did it.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is unsettling: you want to know what will happen, and you can't. In the second volume of Spheres, Globes, Sloterdijk describes how the modern age deprived people of their protective dome. The world used to be imagined as sheltered by heavenly spheres, where everything had its place. When this picture collapsed, human beings found themselves "outside", in an open and unpredictable space. From Sloterdijk's point of view, one could say that your uncertainty is a personal version of the shared experience of modern people, who no longer live under a dome of guarantees. But Sloterdijk also shows the answer: people have learned to build themselves smaller, handmade shelters — homes, habits, circles of loved ones. In an uncertain world you can create a small, reliable climate around yourself.
uncertainty.practice: Name three things that are creating a small, reliable climate around you right now: a place, a person, a habit.

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, results, news — stretches time and makes it hard to concentrate. It is a legitimately hard state. In You Must Change Your Life, Sloterdijk describes the human being as a "practising" creature: our life consists of repetitions that shape us without our noticing. He shows that monks, athletes and musicians turned even empty time into training. Seen this way, one could say that waiting is time whose content you don't control, but whose form you do. You can't speed up the answer. But you can fill the gap with small repeated actions that hold you steady: a walk, breathing, work with your hands. Then waiting becomes not only torment but also an exercise.
waiting.practice: Choose one simple action for the waiting time — take a walk, water the plants, take ten slow breaths. Repeat it whenever the waiting washes over you.

regret.text: Regret over something done or not done can refuse to let go for a long time. Sloterdijk named one of his main books after a line by Rilke — "You must change your life". But he understands change not as sudden repentance but as the long work of practice: people change through repetition, habits, training. Past actions, too, are the result of past exercises — of what circumstances had trained into you. Seen this way, one could say that regret is useful not as self-punishment but as a signpost: here is a skill that was missing back then. Courage, attention, the ability to say "no" or "yes" — all of this can be trained. Sloterdijk reminds us that no one is born ready-made: a master is someone who has made many mistakes.
regret.practice: Write down which skill you were missing back then. Come up with the smallest possible exercise for it this week.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person feels almost like missing a part of yourself. Sloterdijk explains why this is no exaggeration. In the first volume of Spheres, Bubbles, he argues that the human being originally exists not as a loner but "in twos": even before birth we live in a shared space with another, and all our lives we create such paired spheres with those close to us. A beloved person becomes part of the atmosphere you breathe. Seen this way, one could say that longing is the feeling of an empty place in your sphere where the other used to be. The pain speaks of a real bond. And a bubble created by two doesn't vanish at once: its climate, its habits, its words stay with you for a long time.
longing.practice: Recall one detail of the atmosphere you shared with this person — a smell, a phrase, a tune. Let it stay near you for a minute.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — from wars, disasters, injustice — can be almost unbearable. In Stress and Freedom, Sloterdijk describes large societies as "stress communities": they are united by shared worries that the news spreads daily. We all breathe the same atmosphere of alarm. Seen this way, one could say that your pain is not only personal sensitivity but also the fact that you live in air saturated with other people's misfortune. This doesn't mean the pain isn't real; on the contrary, it speaks of your connection with others. But Sloterdijk also points to freedom — the ability to step back from the stream now and then so as not to suffocate. Pain for the world is easier to carry if you also have some clean air: quiet, loved ones, simple tasks.
world_pain.practice: Choose a time of day without news. During that time, do one warm thing for someone near you.

rejection.text: Rejection wounds painfully, and it seems you have been refused everything at once. In Spheres, Sloterdijk shows that a space of closeness — a bubble in which two people breathe shared air — can't be built alone. A sphere arises only when both sides are ready to create it. Seen this way, one could say that rejection is not a verdict on your worth but a sign that a shared bubble didn't form: the other person wasn't ready to enter that space. It hurts, but it is not your failure as a person. Sloterdijk also reminds us of "thymos" — inner dignity. A refusal can wound it, but it doesn't depend on one other person's "no".
rejection.practice: Write down three things that make you worthy of respect regardless of this refusal.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can live in a person deeply and for a long time. Sloterdijk offers an unexpected explanation of its power. In the first volume of Spheres he writes that even before birth we have a first companion — the placenta, an organ we share, from which we are separated right at birth, before we even get to know it. In his view, people spend their whole lives looking for a substitute for this first "other", creating bubbles of closeness. Seen this way, one could say that the fear of being left is very ancient — almost prehistoric for each of us. It doesn't speak of your weakness. But it doesn't predict the future either. You can notice that you have already created new connections many times.
abandonment.practice: Recall three people with whom you had warm connections at different times in your life. Note: I know how to create closeness.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love combines the strength of a feeling with its impossibility — and that is exhausting. In Rage and Time, Sloterdijk argues against the way modern culture sees the human being mainly through "eros" — desire that always lacks something. He reminds us of another side of the soul — "thymos": pride, dignity, generosity, the capacity to give. Seen this way, one could say that in unrequited love eros is left alone, without support: you are entirely in lack. Sloterdijk would suggest remembering thymos: your capacity to love is also your generosity and strength, not only a wound. Leaning on your dignity, you can respect your feeling without letting it determine your worth.
unrequited.practice: Write: "My love shows my generosity in that…" Note where else this generosity could go.

humiliation.text: Humiliation wounds deeply: someone tried to make you smaller. You have a right to this pain. In Rage and Time, Sloterdijk places at the centre "thymos" — the sense of one's own dignity, which demands recognition. Humiliation is a direct blow to thymos, and it's natural that anger, shame and the wish to defend yourself rise in response. Sloterdijk believes these feelings shouldn't be suppressed: they show that dignity is alive. And in Critique of Cynical Reason he recalls Diogenes, who answered the arrogance of the powerful with bodily, cheerful impudence. Seen this way, one could say that humiliation says more about those who humiliated than about you. Your dignity is wounded, but not cancelled.
humiliation.practice: Straighten your back, plant your feet firmly and tell yourself: "My dignity is still with me." Stay in this posture for a minute.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is very common, and there is nothing to be ashamed of in it. Sloterdijk sees the human being as a creature of exercise: we have always worked on ourselves — body, mind, habits. He calls this "anthropotechnics". But he also shows that practice can turn into a whip when "vertical tension" — the pull towards an ideal — becomes a constant reproach. Modern culture offers the body an endless series of unattainable ideals. From Sloterdijk's point of view, one could say that dissatisfaction with your body is a vertical that has stopped inspiring and started to press down. He also recalls Diogenes, who lived in his body without shame, with cheerful freedom. The body is not only a project to be improved but also a home you live in.
body_shame.practice: Make one movement just for the pleasure of it: stretch, roll your shoulders. Don't judge — just feel.

illness.text: Illness, when the body lets you down, takes away strength and familiar possibilities, and you have every right to be angry, sad and tired. In You Must Change Your Life, Sloterdijk writes a great deal about Nietzsche, who was ill for almost his entire life and still found ways to live and think — in the preface to The Gay Science, Nietzsche called his book the gratitude of a convalescent. Sloterdijk sees the human being as a creature able to adapt by creating new exercises for new circumstances. Seen this way, one could say that illness changes which "exercises of life" are available to you, but it doesn't cancel the very capacity to practise. This is not a call to heroism. Sometimes the exercise is simply to rest, to accept help, or to notice one good moment in the day.
illness.practice: Choose one tiny practice for today that is within your strength: five slow breaths out, or a minute by the window. That is enough.

pride.text: Pride in what you have done is a good, deserved feeling. Sloterdijk gives it a special place. In Rage and Time he says that modern culture has become too absorbed in "eros" — desire and lack — and has underestimated "thymos": pride, dignity, joy in one's own strength. For Sloterdijk, thymos is not a vice but a necessary part of a healthy soul. And in You Must Change Your Life he shows that the human being is a creature of exercise: every achievement is the fruit of repetition and effort. Seen this way, one could say that healthy pride is a fair recognition of your training. There's no need to hide it or be ashamed of it. Let yourself enjoy this feeling: it feeds your strength for the next exercises.
pride.practice: Write down how much effort and repetition lay behind this result. Tell yourself: "I trained for this."

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness is a quiet feeling that doesn't need fixing. Sloterdijk opens the first volume of Spheres with the image of a child blowing soap bubbles. The child watches with delight as a bubble floats through the air, as if carrying on the child's own breath — until it bursts. For Sloterdijk, this is an image of all human spaces of closeness: they are beautiful and fragile at once. Seen this way, one could say that gentle sadness is the feeling of someone who sees both the beauty of the bubble and its brevity. There is no despair in it: bubbles burst, but people blow them again and again. Melancholy lets you value what is here now precisely because it is not eternal.
melancholy.practice: Recall a recent moment that was beautiful and has already passed. Stay with it for a minute, as with a bubble you follow with your eyes.
